blocks.html: In a cupping you never say a coffee is bad. You say it is under-extracted, that the acidity is sharp rather than structured, that the finish drops off at eight seconds. That precision is what makes the fix obvious: grind finer, drop the ratio, raise the temperature. The kitchen version of that skill is the one most home cooks never build. They can tell a dish is disappointing. They cannot tell you which axis is off, so they add more seasoning and hope.

You cannot correct what you cannot name. Every correction in cooking is a control action, and a control action needs a measured error signal. It needs something is not an error signal — it is noise. It is about 0.4% under on salt and has no acid at all is an error signal, and it tells you what to add and roughly how much. This module builds the sensor. The rest of the curriculum builds the actuators.

blocks.label: Why calibration beats recipe-following
blocks.html: A recipe is an open-loop controller. It assumes your tomatoes, your salt crystal size, your reduction rate and your pan match the author's — and they do not. A calibrated palate closes the loop: taste, compute the error, correct. That is why two cooks working from the same recipe land a full grade apart, and why the better one stops measuring much after the first year.

This module complements the technical modules — heat, protein, sauces, fermentation — it does not replace them. Technique gets you a dish that is structurally correct; calibration gets you one that is right. And unlike most of the curriculum it is almost entirely no-cook: the whole salt and acid programme runs on the counter with water, a 0.1 g scale and five identical glasses.

sections.title: Mental model — the palate as an instrument

blocks.html: Treat the palate as an instrument with a transfer function: stimulus in, perception out. It is non-linear, it drifts, it saturates, and it has no absolute zero. What it does have — and this is the whole trick — is excellent relative discrimination. You are bad at declaring this is 0.9% salt. You are very good at declaring this one is saltier than that one. Every method here is built to exploit comparison and to avoid asking you for absolute judgements.

Three thresholds matter and they are different numbers. Detection threshold: you notice something is there but cannot name it. Recognition threshold: you can name it — usually two to three times higher. Difference threshold, the just-noticeable difference: how much a stimulus must change before you notice, which is roughly a fixed percentage rather than a fixed amount. For salt that is about 10–20%, which is why moving a soup from 0.80% to 0.85% does nothing you can perceive, and why every correction should be at least 15–20% of the current level.

blocks.title: Instrument specifications — typical trained adult, in water

rows.value: ~0.05–0.1% by weight; recognition near 0.15%
~0.4–0.5% by weight — the least sensitive of the five tastes
~0.002–0.003% — acids read at roughly 200× lower concentration than sugar
~0.01–0.03%; recognition arrives much later because untrained tasters have no label for it

Continuous exposure flattens a channel in 20–60 s; salt and bitter adapt fastest

These are population ranges. Yours will differ — measuring your own is the point of Section 04 onward

blocks.label: Adaptation is not a metaphor
blocks.html: Hold a salty solution in your mouth and perceived saltiness measurably decays within about 30 seconds. Taste six spoons of the same sauce while it reduces and by spoon four you are tasting your adapted baseline, not the sauce. This is why professional kitchens hand the spoon to someone else, and why cuppers slurp, spit and rinse. Fatigue is fast, it is real, and it always biases the same direction: you under-detect what you have been exposed to, so you over-add.

Two further distortions are worth internalising. Temperature: salt and sweetness read weaker when very hot or very cold, so a sauce seasoned perfectly at 85 °C / 185 °F often tastes flat at 20 °C / 68 °F, and a stock corrected straight off the stove is usually over-salted by the time it reaches the plate. Matrix: fat, starch and viscosity slow the delivery of salt and aroma to the receptors, so 1% salt in a thick, fatty sauce reads lower than 1% in a clear broth. Concentration is the variable you control; perception is the variable you measure. They are not the same number, and the gap between them is most of this module.

items.label: L1 · Functional — I taste before serving and I can tell under-salted from correctly salted
L2 · Consistent — I identify which of salt, acid, fat or umami is missing and correct in the right direction
L3 · Optimisation — I size the correction in percent, hit it in one or two moves, and know my own thresholds as numbers
L4 · Mastery — one taste, name the fault, prescribe the fix in grams, and predict how it will read at serving temperature

sections.title: The axes — what each one actually does

blocks.html: Nine axes carry almost everything you will ever need to diagnose. Five are tastes in the strict sense, with receptors on the tongue: salt, acid, sweet, bitter, umami. Three are not tastes at all — fat and richness, heat, and texture are aromatic, tactile or trigeminal — and aroma, delivered retronasally, supplies most of what people call flavour. Balance is a tenth entry and it is not an axis but a relationship between the others. Coffee handed you three of these in high resolution: acidity, bitterness, sweetness, plus body and aroma. Food adds salt, umami, fat and capsaicin as first-class variables, and it adds a moving target — aroma volatilises while you cook, so the dish is never the same measurement twice.

items.title: Salt
items.html: Does: raises perceived intensity of nearly everything, suppresses bitterness, drives aroma into the headspace. The largest effect per gram in the kitchen. Fixes: flat, hollow, missing something. Too much: the dish narrows to one note, the finish turns harsh and slightly metallic, the mouth feels dry. You cannot remove it — only dilute, or move perception with acid.

items.title: Acid
items.html: Does: adds lift and contrast, cuts perceived fat and sweetness, sharpens the outline between components, resets the palate between bites. Fixes: heavy, cloying, muddy, tiring after two bites. Too much: sour attack, shortened finish, and salt starts reading harsh alongside it.

items.title: Sweetness
items.html: Does: rounds edges, suppresses bitterness and sourness, extends the finish, adds a sense of body. Fixes: harsh acid, aggressive bitterness, thin savoury dishes. Too much: reads as sauce-bottle candy and savoury definition collapses. In savoury food the useful dose is often 0.2–0.5% sugar — below its own recognition threshold.

items.title: Bitterness
items.html: Does: adds structure, length and adult seriousness. The most underused axis in home cooking. Fixes: pleasant but forgettable dishes, and over-sweet ones. Too much: drying, astringent, dominating the finish. Unlike coffee, where bitterness usually signals over-extraction, in food it is a deliberate ingredient — char, bitter greens, citrus pith, cacao.

items.title: Umami
items.html: Does: adds savoury depth, body and length; makes a broth taste thicker than the spoon says. Fixes: watery, thin, not enough meat, vegetable dishes with no presence. Too much: a flat sameness and a slightly cloying, drying aftertaste — usually arriving together with too much salt, because every convenient carrier is salty.

items.title: Fat and richness
items.html: Does: dissolves and slowly releases fat-soluble aroma, coats the palate, lengthens the finish, softens capsaicin. Fixes: aromas that vanish, dishes that stop abruptly, excess chilli. Too much: heavy, greasy, and everything else reads muted because delivery has slowed.

items.title: Spice and heat
items.html: Does: trigeminal stimulation, not taste. Adds arousal, perceived intensity and duration. Fixes: monotony, one-dimensional dishes. Too much: capsaicin desensitises the whole instrument for minutes and masks fine detail — you stop being able to judge salt at all.

items.title: Aroma
items.html: Does: supplies the large majority of what people call flavour, almost all of it retronasal. Fixes: correctly seasoned but boring. Too much or wrong: perfumed, soapy, medicinal, muddy. Its defining property is that it leaves: volatiles boil off in seconds to minutes, so timing is part of the dose.

items.title: Texture
items.html: Does: sets the release rate of everything else and sets expectation before a single receptor fires. Fixes: tastes fine, feels wrong; contrast in texture is the cheapest fix for a dull dish. Too much or wrong: gluey, gritty, slimy — and thickening lowers perceived salt at constant sodium.

items.title: Balance
items.html: Does: nothing on its own. It is a relationship, not an ingredient: no axis loud enough to hide the others, and none at zero unless you chose zero. Fixes: nothing directly — you reach it by moving specific axes. Failure mode: chasing balance by adding a bit of everything, which produces the flat, busy, muddy dish that tastes of effort.

blocks.label: The beginner's single-lever reflex
blocks.html: Untrained cooks correct almost everything with salt, because salt is the one lever that produces a large change fast. The result is a whole class of dishes that are simultaneously over-salted and under-flavoured: salt at 1.4%, acid at zero, umami at zero. If your correction reflex fires toward salt more than about two-thirds of the time, you are not diagnosing — you are pulling the only lever you have learned to feel.

sections.title: Setup and method — running a flight properly

blocks.html: A tasting flight is an experiment and it obeys the same rules as any other experiment in this manual: change one variable, hold the rest, record before you compare. Cupping already taught you the format — identical vessels, identical dose, blind where possible, notes written before anyone speaks. Port it directly. The only structural differences are that food samples are heavier, they fatigue the palate faster, and they need a genuinely neutral base to sit in.

rows.value: Something with almost no flavour of its own: filtered water, plain boiled rice, boiled potato, or unsalted stock when you need a food matrix. 500 g is a convenient batch — 1 g of salt in it is exactly 0.2%
Identical, unmarked, all the same colour. Different bowls change expectation, and expectation changes perception by a full point on a five-point scale
Ascending concentration, always. One strong sample contaminates every weaker one that follows it for a minute or more
8–10 g per sample — about two teaspoons. Enough to coat the tongue, small enough to spit
Room-temperature water between every sample, plain bread or an unsalted cracker every third, 45–60 s pause. Longer for fat and capsaicin
Have someone else code the cups, or number the bases and shuffle without looking. Knowing which cup is 1.2% guarantees that you taste 1.2%
Write the note before comparing, before discussing, before checking the labels. Score 0–5 per axis, in numbers
Include one blind duplicate in every flight. If the duplicate scores more than one point apart from its twin, the flight is noise and you rerun it
5–6 samples plus one duplicate. Beyond about ten cups almost nobody is still measuring anything

blocks.html: Two order effects will fool you if you let them. The first is contrast: sample three tastes saltier if sample two was weak and flat if sample two was strong. Ascending order and adequate rinsing bound the damage but never remove it, which is why the duplicate is a control and not a formality. The second is expectation: labels, colour, price and even the shape of the cup shift scores measurably. You already know what a named origin does to a cupping table. Salt is no different, and you are not immune to it.

blocks.label: Spit, and write first
blocks.html: Swallow ten samples and you are calibrating a full stomach rather than a palate. Spit — retronasal aroma still reaches you on the exhale, which is the part that carries most of the information. And write the note before you compare cups or hear anyone else's. The single largest source of self-deception in amateur tasting is revising an impression after seeing the label.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E1 — zero the instrument (triangle test)

fields.detail: Establish that you can actually discriminate at the level you claim, and measure your personal difference threshold for salt as a number.
Same water, same temperature 18–20 °C / 64–68 °F, same vessels, same 8 g dose, same 45 s rinse interval, same time of day.
Three cups per trial, two identical and one different. Start with a wide gap — 0.4% vs 0.8% — then narrow: 0.6 vs 0.8, then 0.7 vs 0.8, then 0.75 vs 0.8.

You will pick the odd cup reliably at a 30–50% relative difference and fall to guessing somewhere around a 10–15% difference. That crossover is your just-noticeable difference, and it sets the smallest correction worth making in any pot.

Hit rate over at least 6 trials per gap. Chance is 1 in 3, so five of six is a real signal and three of six is nothing. Record the gap at which you drop to chance, and the date — you will re-measure this in three months.

blocks.html: Salt is the flagship because it has the largest effect per gram of anything in the kitchen, the narrowest window between correct and ruined, and by far the most counter-intuitive mechanism. The working range for most savoury food is 0.8–1.2% of finished weight. Below about 0.6% food reads flat no matter how good the technique was; above about 1.5% it reads salty and every other axis collapses behind it. In a 500 g pot that entire window is about three grams wide. You are going to find its edges on your own tongue, in numbers, in about forty minutes.

rows.value: 500 g of filtered water at 18–20 °C / 64–68 °F. Run the water version first: it isolates the taste channel from aroma and texture. Repeat later with 500 g of unsalted mashed potato or plain rice for the matrix version
One salt only, weighed, never measured by volume. Fine sea salt or plain table salt without iodine or anti-caking agents — iodine has a detectable metallic note at these concentrations
To waste less, make 100 g portions: 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2 and 1.5 g of salt per 100 g. A 0.1 g scale is mandatory — a 1 g scale physically cannot resolve these steps
8–10 g per cup, identical vessels, coded and shuffled, ascending order on the first pass, one blind duplicate
Four separate numbers 0–5 per sample: perceived saltiness, overall flavour intensity, balance, pleasantness. They do not move together, and that is the entire lesson
45–60 s and a water rinse between cups; plain bread every third; about 40 minutes for the full flight

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E2 — the salt ladder

fields.detail: Find the two numbers that matter: the concentration where perceived flavour intensity peaks, and the concentration where pleasantness starts to fall. They are not the same number, and neither sits where you expect.
One base, one salt, one temperature, identical vessels, 8–10 g per cup, 45 s and a water rinse between samples, plain bread every third cup.
Salt concentration only: 0.3 / 0.6 / 0.9 / 1.2 / 1.5% by weight, plus one blind duplicate inserted at random.

Perceived saltiness rises roughly monotonically. Perceived flavour intensity peaks around 0.9–1.2% and then falls. Pleasantness peaks earlier than saltiness and drops sharply past about 1.2–1.4%. Most people place their personal correct point between 0.8% and 1.1%.

Plot all four scores against concentration on one sheet. The gap between the saltiness curve and the intensity curve is the region where salt is working for you invisibly — that region is the whole point of the exercise. Also check your duplicate: if the twins differ by more than one point, rerun.

blocks.html:
Why salt raises flavour before it tastes salty

Three mechanisms stack, and none of them is salt tastes good.

  • Bitter suppression. Sodium ions interfere with bitter transduction at the receptor. Removing bitterness from the mix unmasks sweetness and aroma that were there all along, so the dish reads richer without anything having been added to those channels.
  • Cross-modal enhancement. Sodium raises perceived sweetness and, strongly, perceived umami. Salt and glutamate are close to multiplicative: the same broth at 0.4% and at 0.9% salt does not taste twice as salty, it tastes like it has more meat in it.
  • Physical aroma release. Dissolved salt lowers the solubility of many volatile compounds in water — the salting-out effect — pushing them into the headspace and up into the nose retronasally. More aroma molecules reach the olfactory epithelium per bite. Since aroma supplies most of perceived flavour, this alone accounts for a large share of the effect.

The consequence is the most useful single fact in this module: there is a band, roughly 0.5–0.9%, in which salt measurably improves the dish while staying below your recognition threshold for salt itself. Inside that band your brain has no label for what changed, so it reports better with no cause attached. Above roughly 1.3% you have crossed into salt-as-a-flavour, and the other axes start losing.

blocks.label: Why under-salted food gets called missing something
blocks.html: Because it is literally missing several things and none of them has salt's name on it. The bitterness that salt would have suppressed is still present. The aroma that salt would have driven into the headspace is still in solution. The umami is reading at half strength. Not one of those absences announces itself as salt — they present as a general dullness with no address. That is why the person eating says it needs something, and why the cook, hearing no specific complaint, reaches for pepper.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E3 — the invisible band, in real food

fields.detail: Prove the sub-threshold effect in a food matrix rather than in water: show that salt below your recognition threshold still raises measured flavour intensity.
One batch of plain tomato sauce or unsalted chicken broth split into four identical 200 g portions, all served at 60–65 °C / 140–150 °F, same bowls, blind and shuffled.
Salt only: 0.2%, 0.5%, 0.8% and 1.1% — that is 0.4 g, 1.0 g, 1.6 g and 2.2 g per 200 g portion.

You will score the 0.5% and 0.8% samples as clearly more flavourful and more tomato-like while still not describing either as salty. Many tasters cannot correctly rank the samples by salt content while confidently ranking them by flavour.

Score saltiness and flavour intensity as two separate numbers, then attempt to rank the cups by actual salt content and compare against the true order. Ranking errors here are the finding, not a failure — they are the direct measurement of the invisible band.

blocks.label: Where salt calibration goes wrong
blocks.html: Four failures, in order of how often they happen. Volume dosing: a teaspoon of flaky salt and a teaspoon of fine salt differ by up to a factor of two in mass — weigh it. Correcting hot: perceived saltiness is lower at high temperature, so a sauce corrected at a rolling boil typically lands 0.1–0.2% over once plated. Ignoring reduction: salt does not evaporate. A sauce seasoned to 0.9% and then reduced by a third is at 1.35% and is finished — season after reduction, not before. Serial tasting: by the fifth spoon you are adapted and will push in another 20% that nobody else will enjoy.

Acid is the axis that separates food which is technically seasoned from food which is alive. It works by contrast: it cuts perceived fat, shortens the impression of sweetness, sharpens the boundary between components, and resets the palate between bites so the third bite is as vivid as the first. Coffee gives you a head start — you already distinguish a structured malic brightness from a flat sourness. Food acids differ in one important respect: each arrives with its own aroma load, so you must match acidity before you can compare aromas honestly. Otherwise you are measuring your pouring hand.

rows.value: Vinegar at 5% and lime at 5.5% are close, but a splash of each is not the same dose. Unmatched samples measure your pouring hand, not the ingredient
Dilute every acid to a nominal 1% in water, then dose all samples at the same weight. Errors of ±10% do not matter here; errors of 2× destroy the comparison
Matching by pH is tempting and wrong. pH measures free hydrogen ions; perceived sourness tracks total titratable acidity. A weak acid at the same pH tastes markedly more sour

Most finished savoury dishes land near 0.2–0.5% added acid by weight. A 500 g sauce usually wants 5–15 g of a 5% acid — one to three teaspoons — which is far less than beginners expect and far more than they dare
Acid last, off the heat, in two doses. The acidity survives cooking; the brightness does not

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E4 — five acids at matched strength

fields.detail: Separate what acid does structurally from what a particular acid smells like, and measure how acid moves the other axes at constant salt.
One base — 500 g of broth or plain tomato base held at exactly 0.8% salt — same temperature, same vessels, same 8–10 g sample, same total acid dose in every acidified cup.
Five cups: no acid as control, then lime, white vinegar, rice vinegar and cider vinegar, each pre-diluted to a nominal 1% acidity and dosed at 3% of sample weight.

All four acidified cups read brighter and less heavy than the control. They also read less salty at identical salt, because acid and salt suppress each other. Lime brings the largest aroma change and the shortest-lived one; white vinegar is the cleanest acid signal with almost no aroma; rice vinegar reads softest at equal acidity.

Score sourness, perceived saltiness, perceived richness, brightness and finish length for each cup. The interesting column is perceived saltiness: that number moves while the actual sodium is constant across all five cups.

blocks.html:
The interactions are why acid deserves this much attention.

  • Acid and salt suppress each other. Add acid to a dish sitting at 1.3% salt and it stops reading over-salted; add salt to something too sour and the sourness recedes. This is the standard rescue for a dish pushed slightly past the salt line — you cannot remove sodium, but you can move perception.
  • Acid cuts perceived fat and sweetness. A braise at the point of being tiring becomes drinkable with 0.3% added acid, and every gram of fat is still in the pot. Nothing was removed; contrast was restored.
  • Sweetness rounds acid. Two grams of sugar in 500 g will not make a sauce sweet, but it will pull a sharp acid attack back into structure. It is the same move as a touch of sugar in a harsh, over-extracted coffee: mask the edge, keep the body.
  • Acid shortens the finish. Usually a feature. When it is not — when the dish now stops abruptly — the correction is fat or umami, not less acid.

blocks.label: Acid off the heat, in two moves
blocks.html: Half the dose, taste 30 seconds later, then the rest if it still wants it. Acid crosses from not-enough to sour in a smaller window than salt does, and unlike salt it cannot be hidden behind the other axes once it is loud. On the stove the acidity stays while the aroma boils off, so lime added at the start contributes sourness only. That may be exactly what you want — decide it deliberately rather than by accident.

Umami is the axis your coffee training did not give you. It is the taste of free glutamate and of certain nucleotides — inosinate from meat and fish, guanylate from dried mushrooms — and its subjective signature is less a flavour than a property: length, body, mouth-filling savouriness, the sense that a broth is thicker than the spoon says. Untrained tasters almost never name it. They say deep, meaty, rich, more-ish, or they credit fat that is not in the pot. Learning to hear it as a separate channel is the largest single upgrade available to anyone who cooks vegetables.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E5 — glutamate and the synergy multiplier

fields.detail: Hear umami as its own channel, then measure the glutamate-nucleotide synergy directly rather than taking it on faith.

500 g of weak unsalted vegetable broth split into five 100 g portions, every one brought to exactly 0.6% salt so that salt is not the variable, all served at 60–65 °C / 140–150 °F, identical cups, blind and shuffled.

A: control, salt only. B: plus 0.5% soy sauce. C: plus 0.5% dried shiitake soaking liquid, which is nucleotide-rich and glutamate-poor. D: plus 0.25% soy and 0.25% shiitake liquid — half the total addition of B and C. E: plus 1% soy.

Sample D, with half the total additive, should read as deep as or deeper than B and often deeper than E. That is the synergy: glutamate together with inosinate or guanylate is multiplicative rather than additive, with reported enhancement up to roughly 8× at favourable ratios. C alone reads thin and slightly odd, because nucleotides do very little on their own.

Score savoury depth, body, finish length and saltiness. Watch the saltiness column: it drifts upward with umami even though every cup is fixed at 0.6% salt. That drift is the reason umami and salt must be calibrated together.

blocks.html: The synergy is worth understanding mechanically, because it changes how you build a stock. Glutamate binds the umami receptor; the nucleotides bind an adjacent site and stabilise the receptor in its active conformation, so a small quantity of nucleotide sharply raises the response to whatever glutamate is already present. In practice that is why nearly every traditional broth on earth is a glutamate source plus a nucleotide source: kombu with katsuobushi, tomato with beef, Parmesan rind with chicken, dried mushroom with soy, onion with dried shrimp. None of those cuisines had the biochemistry. They had calibrated palates and several centuries.

blocks.label: Why untrained palates read umami as depth
blocks.html: Salt, sweet, sour and bitter all have a sharp temporal signature — they arrive and they leave. Umami is slow: low intensity, long duration, spread across the whole tongue, and it lingers after swallowing. A stimulus with no sharp onset never gets filed as an event, so the brain attributes it to the dish as a whole rather than to an ingredient. That is exactly why fish sauce at 0.5% is simultaneously invisible and indispensable — nobody tastes fish sauce, and everybody notices when you leave it out.

blocks.label: The salt ceiling on umami
blocks.html: Every convenient umami source is also a salt source. Push soy sauce to 3% of dish weight and you have added about 0.5% salt with it — half your budget — while the umami is nowhere near its ceiling. Calibrate the two together: dose the umami carrier first, compute the salt it brought, then top up with plain salt to your 0.8–1.0% target. Cooks who do this in the other order end up salty and still shallow, which is the most common seasoning failure above beginner level.

sections.title: Fat, texture and heat — the axes that are not tastes

blocks.html: Three of the nine axes are not tastes at all, and treating them as tastes is exactly why they get mismanaged. Fat is a solvent and a texture. Texture is a rate controller. Capsaicin is pain. None of the three has a receptor on the tongue reporting flavour, yet together they determine how much of everything else you perceive and for how long. In coffee you met a weak version of this in body and mouthfeel. In food it is a first-order effect, large enough to make two dishes with identical chemistry score a point apart.

items.title: Fat as a solvent
items.html: Most of the aroma compounds that matter — pyrazines from browning, terpenes from herbs, capsaicinoids, carotenoid-derived notes — are fat-soluble and water-shy. Fat dissolves them, holds them, and releases them slowly across the whole bite. Remove the fat and the aroma does not merely weaken, it changes shape: a sharp early peak and then nothing. That is why a fat-free version of a good sauce tastes thin and oddly harsh at the same time.

items.title: Fat as time
items.html: Fat is the main lever on finish length. A sauce that stops abruptly while being correctly salted and correctly acidified is usually short on fat. Mounting 5–15 g of butter or oil into 500 g of sauce off the heat lengthens the finish measurably without reading as greasy, because emulsified fat is perceived as body rather than as oil.

items.title: Viscosity as a rate controller
items.html: Thickening a liquid slows the diffusion of salt, acid and aroma to the receptors. The same 1% salt reads perceptibly lower in a starch-thickened sauce than in a thin one — commonly by the equivalent of 0.1–0.2% salt. If you thicken after seasoning you will have to reseason; if you season after thickening, taste at the final consistency or do not bother tasting.

items.title: Structure and expectation
items.html: Texture sets expectation before a single taste receptor fires. Grit, sliminess and gumminess get scored as flavour faults by almost every taster even when the seasoning is identical. Crunch does the reverse: textural contrast raises the perceived intensity of the whole dish and is the cheapest available fix for correct but boring.

items.title: Capsaicin is trigeminal
items.html: Capsaicin binds TRPV1, the same receptor that reports temperatures above about 43 °C / 109 °F. Your brain is not tasting chilli, it is receiving heat and pain from the trigeminal nerve. Four consequences: it accumulates instead of adapting away, it takes minutes rather than seconds to clear, it is fat-soluble so water does nothing while dairy works, and it desensitises the whole region while active — which is why you cannot judge salt in a dish you have just over-chillied.

items.title: Temperature and astringency
items.html: Serving temperature moves salt and sweet perception by a real margin, so season at serving temperature or apply a known offset. Astringency — the drying, puckering feel from tannins in unripe fruit, tea, red wine, some beans — is tactile rather than taste, and it stacks with bitterness. Fat and sweetness both mask it; acid does not, and often makes it worse.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E6 — fat, viscosity and the perception of salt

fields.detail: Measure how much of what you call seasoning is actually delivery, by moving fat and viscosity while holding sodium exactly constant.
600 g of unsalted broth divided into three 200 g portions, every one salted to exactly 0.9%, same aromatics, same temperature 60–65 °C / 140–150 °F, same bowls, blind and shuffled.
A: broth as it is. B: broth plus 3% fat — 6 g of butter or oil, emulsified with a stick blender so it does not separate. C: broth thickened with a 1.5% cornstarch slurry and no added fat.

All three contain identical salt. B reads rounder, longer and usually slightly less salty, with more herb aroma. C reads clearly less salty and less aromatic — often by the equivalent of 0.1–0.2% salt — and flatter overall. Most tasters will insist the three cups have different salt levels.

Score saltiness, aroma intensity, body and finish length, then reveal that sodium was constant. Write down how large the perceptual error was in salt-equivalent terms. That number is your personal correction factor for thick and rich dishes, and you should apply it deliberately from then on.

blocks.html: The practical rules that fall out of this are short. Season at final consistency and final temperature, or apply the offset you just measured. Add delicate aroma late — fresh herbs, citrus zest, finishing oil — because volatiles leave a hot pan on a timescale of seconds to minutes and a dish can lose most of its top notes in the last five minutes of a simmer. Treat chilli as a separate decision taken after the dish is balanced, since once capsaicin is in the system your instrument is degraded for the rest of the session. And when a dish tastes muted but measures correct on salt and acid, suspect delivery — fat, temperature, or a sauce thickened too far — before you add more of anything.

blocks.label: Chilli last, and never mid-flight
blocks.html: Capsaicin does not fade over 30 seconds the way salt adaptation does; it accumulates and needs several minutes to clear, and dairy clears it far faster than water because casein strips capsaicin from the receptor and fat dissolves it. If you are running a calibration flight, place every capsaicin sample at the end and accept that the session ends when they do. Locally this also means knowing your peppers as measurements: chiltoma is a sweet pepper carrying essentially no capsaicin and is an aromatic decision, while chile congo sits in the hundreds of thousands of Scoville units and is a trigeminal one. Confusing the two categories is how a balanced dish becomes unjudgeable in one spoonful.

sections.title: Building a vocabulary — from cupping to cooking

blocks.html: Vocabulary is not decoration, it is the addressing scheme. A word that maps to a specific correction is useful; a word that does not is noise. Delicious is noise. Under-salted with a short finish addresses two specific levers. Coffee already gave you half the system: a working lexicon for acidity, body, sweetness, aftertaste and cleanliness, plus the habit of scoring on a scale instead of arguing in adjectives. The transfer is mostly direct, with three places where it is actively misleading.

head: Coffee descriptor
Food equivalent
Same, or where it diverges
rows: Acidity as a quality — structured, malic, citric
Same idea, wider range. In coffee acidity is intrinsic to the bean and the extraction; in food you dose it deliberately, and each acid arrives with its own aroma
Same axis, different drivers. Coffee body comes from oils and fines; food body comes from fat, gelatine, starch and emulsification, which you control independently of everything else
Different scale entirely. Coffee sweetness is a subtle perception near threshold; food sweetness is often a deliberate ingredient well above it
Diverges hard. In coffee bitterness normally signals over-extraction and gets corrected away; in food it is a structural axis you deliberately add — char, bitter greens, citrus pith, cacao
Same, and equally diagnostic. A short finish in food usually means low fat or low umami, not over-extraction
Clarity — no muddiness, each component identifiable
Same concept. In food, muddiness usually comes from too many aromatics, over-reduction, or oxidised fat
Same word, more axes. Coffee balances three or four variables; food balances at least nine, and two of them are not tastes
Same discipline, and weighing plus recording is what makes it possible in both
Coffee has no salt axis at all. This is the single largest gap in a cupper's vocabulary arriving at food, and it happens to be the most important axis
None of these exists meaningfully in coffee. Expect to have no words for them for the first few weeks and to borrow depth, heat and body until better ones arrive

blocks.html:
The three-part note

Record every impression as intensity, quality and position in time. Intensity is a number 0–5, not a word. Quality is the descriptor: which acid, which kind of bitterness, whether the salt reads clean or metallic. Position is when it happens — attack in the first second, mid-palate, or finish. Bitter is useless. Bitterness 3, drying, only in the finish points you at over-reduction or burnt aromatics. Bitterness 3, on the attack points at the ingredient itself.

Then add one line the cupping form does not have: the prescription. What you would change, by how much, on which axis. Even when the prescription turns out wrong, writing it down converts a vague impression into a testable prediction, and testable predictions are the only mechanism by which a palate actually improves.

blocks.title: A note format that is still useful six months later

rows.value: What it was, which batch, and the exact concentrations if you know them
Temperature, time of day, what you ate or drank in the previous hour, whether it was blind, who else was tasting
Salt, acid, sweet, bitter, umami, fat, heat, aroma, texture — nine numbers, each 0–5. Fifteen seconds
Descriptor plus position in time, in that order. Two or three lines maximum
The correction you would make, with a number attached: +0.15% salt, 2 g of lime, hold everything else
What actually happened when you applied it. This is the field that converts tasting into calibration, and it is the one everybody skips

blocks.label: Numbers before adjectives
blocks.html: Score first, describe second. The moment you write brothy and warming you are committed to a story, and every later observation bends toward it. Scoring nine axes 0–5 takes fifteen seconds and produces something you can average, compare across sessions and plot against concentration. Adjectives are for communicating a result to another person. Numbers are for calibrating yourself, and you are the instrument under calibration.

sections.title: Troubleshooting — instrument faults and dish faults

blocks.html: Five failures cover most of what goes wrong, and four of them are instrument faults rather than food faults. Treat each one as data: the diagnosis is worth more than the fix, because the fix only rescues tonight while the diagnosis changes every session after it.

blocks.problem: Everything tastes flat, and adding salt does not help

fields.detail: Usually two axes at zero rather than one axis low: no acid and no umami, with salt already at or above 1%. Sometimes it is delivery — a sauce thickened past the point where salt reaches the receptors, or food served at a temperature that suppresses salt and sweet perception. Occasionally it is you: a cold, a strong coffee twenty minutes ago, toothpaste within the hour.

Split a spoonful three ways on separate saucers. Add a grain of salt to the first, two drops of lime to the second, three drops of soy or a smear of miso to the third. Taste the untouched original, then all three, then the original again. Whichever saucer wakes up names your missing axis in about twenty seconds.

Correct the axis the split test identified, in a step of at least 15–20% of the current level so the change clears your difference threshold. Acid saucer wins: dose 0.2–0.3% acid off the heat, in two moves. Umami saucer wins: add the carrier first, then recompute salt, since the carrier brought some. If none of the three moved, the fault is fat, temperature or aroma — mount 2–3% fat off the heat and taste again at actual serving temperature.

blocks.problem: It tastes salty but still boring

fields.detail: The salt axis has been used as a substitute for the other eight. Salt is above roughly 1.2% while acid, umami, fat, aroma and texture sit near zero — the standard outcome of correcting by reflex instead of by diagnosis. A second cause is reduction: the dish was seasoned correctly, then lost water, and salt does not evaporate. A third is aroma loss, which leaves the non-volatile salt behind and nothing else.

Score the nine axes 0–5 honestly. If salt is 4 and nothing else is above 2, this is the fault and not a matter of taste. Then check the pot: did the volume drop noticeably after you seasoned it? A third reduction turns 0.9% into 1.35%.

You cannot remove sodium, so change the ratios instead. Dilute with unsalted base if any exists — adding 20% unsalted stock takes 1.3% down to about 1.08%. Then add acid, which lowers perceived saltiness at constant sodium, and add fat and fresh aroma to widen and lengthen the dish. Next time, dose umami and acid first and reserve salt for the final correction, after reduction is finished.

blocks.problem: I cannot tell the samples apart

fields.detail: Either the difference is genuinely below your just-noticeable difference — under roughly 10–15% relative on salt — or the method is leaking. Common leaks: samples at different temperatures, different vessels, descending concentration order, no rinse between cups, scoring after discussing with someone. Occasionally the samples are simply too small or too cold to release any aroma.

Run a triangle test with a deliberately wide gap, 0.4% against 0.8%. If you call that reliably, your instrument is fine and the flight design was too tight or contaminated. If you cannot call even that, the problem is your current state or the conditions, not your ability — check hydration, recent coffee, illness, and the temperature of the samples.

Widen the steps to at least 1.5× — 0.4, 0.6, 0.9, 1.35 — until you can call them, then narrow again by stages. Fix the mechanics at the same time: identical vessels, identical temperature, ascending order, 45–60 s and a water rinse between samples, note written before any comparison. Add a blind duplicate and treat the spread between the twins as your noise floor: no result smaller than that spread means anything.

blocks.problem: My palate died halfway through the flight

fields.detail: Adaptation and fatigue, which are physiological and entirely predictable. Salt and bitter channels flatten within 20–60 s of continuous exposure. Capsaicin, strong bitters, very fatty samples and anything above about 1.5% salt will degrade the rest of the session. And ten or more samples in one sitting is beyond almost everyone regardless of training.

Re-taste sample one at the end, blind, and compare against its original score. If it now scores more than one point different, the session drifted and everything after roughly the midpoint is unreliable. This is exactly what the blind duplicate is for.

Cap flights at 5–6 samples plus one duplicate. Rinse with room-temperature water between every sample and eat plain bread or an unsalted cracker every third. Allow 60–120 s between samples and a five-minute break at the midpoint. Order ascending and put fat, bitter and capsaicin samples last. Then stop: a second short session tomorrow produces better data than a long one today.

blocks.problem: It tasted right in the pot and flat on the plate

fields.detail: Temperature is the usual culprit: salt and sweet perception fall as food cools, so a sauce corrected at 90 °C / 194 °F is under-seasoned by the time it is eaten at 55 °C / 130 °F. The second cause is dilution by the rest of the plate — a sauce seasoned to taste on its own lands near 0.6% once it meets unsalted rice. The third is aroma loss between the pan and the table, which is a delivery failure rather than a seasoning one.

Take two spoonfuls. Taste one immediately, let the other sit four minutes, taste it, and record the difference in scores. That gap is your personal temperature bias, and it is repeatable. Separately, weigh the sauce against the starch it will dress and compute the combined salt percentage before you decide anything.

Season components in the ratio in which they will actually be eaten, and taste anything served cool at its serving temperature. A sauce meant to dress a bland starch should be seasoned above the 0.9% target — 1.2–1.4% is normal for something that will be diluted roughly twofold. Finish aroma at the last possible moment, on the plate if necessary.

blocks.html: Calibration is not something you do once. Thresholds shift with health, hydration, sleep, medication and how much salt you have been eating this month, and the only defence is a short repeatable flight run often enough to catch the drift. One of these is weekly and takes ten minutes. The rest are one-offs that build the reference library you will be tasting against for the next decade.

blocks.eyebrow: Practice drill · L1 to L2 · 10 minutes, weekly
blocks.title: Weekly two-point calibration

fields.detail: Maintain a stable internal reference for salt and detect drift in your own instrument before it reaches your cooking.
Beginner, but worthless unless it is actually repeated. Put it on the same day each week.
A 0.1 g scale, three identical opaque cups, filtered water, one salt, a notebook.

Make 200 g of water at 0.6% (1.2 g salt), 200 g at 0.9% (1.8 g) and 200 g at 1.2% (2.4 g). Have someone code and shuffle them, or number the bases and shuffle without looking. Rank them by saltiness, then write down which one you would call correctly seasoned — before you check the codes.
Correct ranking three weeks running, and your personal correct point lands within ±0.1% of where it landed last week.
Guessing order from cup position · tasting warm one week and cold the next · running it right after coffee or toothpaste · skipping the written prediction, which is the only part that catches drift.

If the ranking is unreliable, widen to 0.4 / 0.9 / 1.4% until it stabilises, then narrow again. If it is trivially easy, tighten to 0.75 / 0.9 / 1.05% — a 20% step, right at the edge of the difference threshold.

blocks.title: Blind triangle ladder, one axis at a time

fields.detail: Find, and then lower, your difference threshold on each axis separately, so you know which channel is your weakest.
Intermediate — needs a second person or genuinely disciplined self-blinding.
Scale, six to nine identical cups, water, salt, white vinegar, sugar, and a glutamate source such as soy sauce or instant dashi.

Pick one axis per session. Prepare three cups, two identical and one different, at a chosen relative gap. Identify the odd cup. Run six trials at that gap, then reduce the gap and repeat. Record hit rate per gap in a table, with the date.
Five or more correct out of six at a 15% relative gap on salt, and a documented threshold number for at least three axes.
Fewer than six trials per gap, so luck looks like skill · changing two things between trials · running more than about twelve cups in a session · scoring after you already peeked.
Train the axis where your threshold is worst. For most people arriving from coffee that is umami, then salt. Retest the same axis a month later and compare the numbers, not the feeling.

blocks.eyebrow: Practice drill · L2 to L3 · on real food
blocks.title: Split-spoon diagnosis

fields.detail: Compress diagnosis to under thirty seconds so it is usable at the stove, not only at a tasting bench.
Intermediate.
Any dish you are genuinely cooking, four small saucers, salt, an acid, an umami carrier, a fat.

Take four small portions of the dish. Leave one untouched as the control. Add a measured micro-dose to each of the other three: salt, acid, umami carrier. Taste the control, then each saucer, then the control again. Write your prescription before you touch the pot.
Your prediction of which axis the pot needs matches the split-test result at least four times in five, and the corrected dish needs no second correction.

Doses too large to compare · forgetting to re-taste the control at the end · correcting the pot before finishing the test · using a fourth saucer for fat and then judging it hot, when fat needs serving temperature to be judged.

Log every prescription and its outcome. After twenty entries you will find one systematic bias — most people either chronically under-acidify or chronically over-salt — and knowing which one you are is worth more than any recipe you will ever read.

blocks.title: Season it blind, let someone else judge

fields.detail: Season a simple dish to your target with no measuring after the base is made, then have another person score it blind against two deliberately mis-seasoned versions — one 25% under on salt, one 25% over — without knowing which is which.
Absolute seasoning judgement, correcting under time pressure, separating your own adapted preference from a general target, and taking sensory feedback as data rather than as criticism.

A rice, bean or soup base split into three portions: yours seasoned to taste, one at 0.75× your salt level, one at 1.25×. The judge ranks all three for pleasantness and then guesses which is which. Run it four weeks running with the same judge, and keep the numbers.

You pass when your version is ranked first in at least three of the four rounds and the judge correctly identifies the over-salted sample — which together mean your target is close to a general one rather than to your own adaptation. If your version consistently loses to the 0.75× sample, your palate has drifted salty and the weekly two-point drill is the correction.
Convert loose impressions into a written personal standard: your own thresholds, your own targets by dish type, and an error log with outcomes attached.
Structured recording, self-calibration, honesty about small sample sizes, and translating perception into numeric prescriptions.

One document in four parts. (1) Your measured detection and difference thresholds for salt, acid, sweet, bitter and umami, with dates. (2) Your preferred salt percentage for at least six dish types — soup, sauce, braise, rice, dressing, grilled protein. (3) A comparison sheet for five acids and five umami carriers at matched strength, with aroma notes. (4) A log of at least twenty prescription-and-outcome entries.

The document is finished when you can pick an unfamiliar recipe, predict its salt target within ±0.15% before tasting anything, and be right more often than not. Re-measure the thresholds every three months; if any has moved more than about 20%, something in your diet or health changed and every target in the document needs re-anchoring.

blocks.html: These are not recall questions. Each one is answerable only if the mechanism is genuinely understood. If you find yourself reciting a number instead of explaining a cause, go back to the experiment it came from and run it again — the number is worthless without the mechanism attached to it.

questions: Why does an under-salted dish usually get described as missing something rather than as not salty enough? Name at least two mechanisms and say which one you think dominates in a clear broth versus in a fatty braise.

You have 500 g of sauce at 1.3% salt that reads over-salted, and there is no unsalted base left to dilute it with. Name two changes that will make it read correctly, explain why they work when the sodium content has not moved, and say which one shortens the finish.

Two broths contain identical salt at 0.9%. One is thickened with starch, one is not. Predict which reads saltier, estimate the size of the difference in salt-equivalent terms, and explain the mechanism in one sentence.
Why is a single blind duplicate in a flight worth more than adding a sixth concentration level? Answer in terms of what each addition actually measures.

In the umami experiment, sample D contains half the total additive of samples B and E yet often scores deepest. Explain what is happening at the receptor, and name two traditional pairings from any cuisine that exploit the same effect.

You add the same weight of lime juice to a stew, once at the start of a 40-minute simmer and once off the heat at the end. The two results will not taste the same. State precisely what differs, what stays the same, and which of the two you would choose for a rich pork braise and why.

blocks.label: L3 · Optimisation — the exit condition for this module
Exit criteria
blocks.html: You are done here when three things are true. You can rank a blind three-point salt ladder at 20% steps, reliably, on demand. You can taste an unfamiliar dish once and write a prescription with a number attached — +0.15% salt and 3 g of lime, nothing else — that turns out to be right more often than not. And you have twenty logged prescription-and-outcome entries, because until the outcomes are written down you have opinions rather than calibration. Then keep running the ten-minute weekly drill for the rest of your cooking life. The instrument drifts, and it never tells you that it has.

title: The Calibrated Palate
lede: You already know how to calibrate a sensory instrument — cupping taught you that. This module ports the discipline to food, where the axes multiply: salt, acid, sweetness, bitterness, umami, fat, heat, aroma and texture all move at once, and aroma keeps evaporating while you work. The goal is not a better recipe. It is a palate that names the fault in one taste and prescribes the correction in grams.
